rows.stem:
(a) Define Effective collision.
(b) Write the unit of
(i) second order reaction and (ii) zero order reaction
rows.solution:
(a) An effective collision is one that actually results in the formation of products. Most collisions do not: for a collision to be effective the colliding molecules must carry energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and they must also be correctly oriented at the moment of impact. The vast majority of collisions fail one condition or the other, which is why reaction rates are so much smaller than collision frequencies.

(b) The units follow from the rate law, since the rate itself always carries units of mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).
(i) For a second order reaction rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^2\), so \(k\) = rate divided by concentration squared: \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\).
(ii) For a zero order reaction rate \(= k\), so \(k\) carries the units of rate itself: mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

The question says "the unit of a second order reaction" without specifying the rate CONSTANT, and the marking scheme accordingly also accepts mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) for part (i) — the units of the reaction's RATE, which are the same for every order. It is the rate constant whose units change with the order, which is what makes the question worth asking.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) Why second ionization enthalpies of chromium and copper are exceptionally higher than those of their neighbouring elements ?
(b) Why transition elements form interstitial compounds ?
rows.solution:
(a) The second ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from the \(\mathrm{M^{+}}\) ion, and for these two metals that ion is unusually stable. Chromium is \(3d^5 4s^1\), so \(\mathrm{Cr^{+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell. Copper is \(3d^{10} 4s^1\), so \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — a completely filled one. Both arrangements have extra stability, so breaking into them to remove a second electron costs far more than it does for their neighbours, whose \(\mathrm{M^{+}}\) ions have no such configuration.

(b) Because transition metals have relatively large atoms whose crystal lattices contain sizeable voids, and small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and boron can fit into those voids without disturbing the lattice. The resulting interstitial compounds are non-stoichiometric, very hard, with high melting points, and they retain metallic conductivity. Steel and cast iron, which are interstitial compounds of iron with carbon, are the industrially important examples.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the major product in the following reaction :
Chlorobenzene \(+\ \mathrm{CH_3-Cl} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Na}}\) ?
(b) What happens when 2-Bromobutane is made to react with alcoholic potassium hydroxide ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a)'s first reactant is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a plain benzene hexagon with three alternating inner double bonds carrying a single Cl at the top vertex and no other substituent, i.e. chlorobenzene. Read on my own page at 4.5x. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) This is the Wurtz-Fittig reaction, which couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide using sodium in dry ether. The new bond forms between the two carbons that carried the halogens, so a methyl group is attached to the benzene ring:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)
The major product is toluene.

(b) With ALCOHOLIC potassium hydroxide the reaction is elimination, not substitution: the hydroxide acts as a base, removing a \(\beta\) hydrogen along with the bromide, and an alkene is formed.
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{KOH\ (alc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CH_3} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The major product is but-2-ene, since by Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene predominates; but-1-ene is formed as the minor product. Aqueous potassium hydroxide would instead have substituted, giving butan-2-ol.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
60 g of glucose is dissolved in 250 g of water. Calculate the freezing point of this solution.
(molar mass of glucose = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = 1.86 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Glucose is a non-volatile, non-electrolytic solute, so no van't Hoff factor is needed.
\(\Delta T_f = K_f \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A}\)
\(= 1.86 \times \dfrac{60}{180} \times \dfrac{1000}{250}\)
\(= \dfrac{7.44}{3} = 2.48\ \mathrm{K}\)

The depression is subtracted from the freezing point of the pure solvent:
\(T_f = T_f^{\circ} - \Delta T_f = 273.15 - 2.48 = 270.67\ \mathrm{K}\)
that is \(-2.48\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(a) Complete and balance the following equations :
(i) \(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
(ii) \(5\mathrm{S^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 16\mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
(b) Why is chemistry of actinoids complicated as compared to lanthanoids ?
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Chromate and dichromate are interconvertible, and the pH decides which is present. Acidifying converts the yellow chromate to the orange dichromate; chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout, so this is not a redox change.
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(ii) Permanganate oxidises sulphide to free sulphur in acid solution and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(5\mathrm{S^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{S}\)

(b) Two things complicate actinoid chemistry. They are all radioactive, so they are hazardous to handle and several exist only in minute artificially prepared amounts. And they show a much wider range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids, because their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie so close in energy that comparable numbers of electrons can be lost from all three — uranium runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\), where the lanthanoids are overwhelmingly \(+3\).

rows.stem:
(a) Explain why \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) is strongly paramagnetic whereas \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) is weakly paramagnetic. [Atomic number of Fe = 26]
(b) On the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion for which \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
rows.solution:
(a) Iron is \(+3\) in both complexes, so \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\) in both; only the ligand field differs, and it changes how many of those five electrons stay unpaired.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) water is a weak field ligand, so the crystal field splitting is smaller than the pairing energy. The five electrons occupy all five d orbitals singly, leaving FIVE unpaired, and the complex is strongly paramagnetic.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) cyanide is a strong field ligand, so the splitting exceeds the pairing energy. The electrons crowd into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set and pair as far as they can, leaving only ONE unpaired, so the complex is only weakly paramagnetic.

(b) When \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) the field is weak, so promoting an electron into the upper set costs less than pairing two in the lower one. A \(d^5\) ion therefore places one electron in each of the five orbitals:
\(t_{2g}^3\ e_g^2\)
This is the high spin arrangement, with all five electrons unpaired — the maximum possible for a d ion.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given compound :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)CH(Br)CH_3}\)
(b) Define Racemisation.
(c) The boiling points of the alkyl halides with the same alkyl group decrease in the given order :
\(\mathrm{RI > RBr > RCl > RF}\)
Explain the above statement.
rows.solution:
(a) The longest chain is four carbons, so the parent is butane, with a methyl branch and a bromine on it. Numbering from either end gives the substituent locants \(\{2, 3\}\), so the tie is broken by the alphabetical rule: the substituent cited first alphabetically gets the lower number, and bromo comes before methyl. The name is 2-bromo-3-methylbutane.

(b) Racemisation is the conversion of a single pure enantiomer into a racemic mixture — an equimolar mixture of both enantiomers, which is optically inactive because their equal and opposite rotations cancel.

(c) All four alkyl halides are held together by van der Waals forces, and the strength of those forces grows with the size and the mass of the atom, since a larger, more polarisable electron cloud is more easily distorted into the temporary dipoles that produce them. Iodine is the largest and heaviest halogen here and fluorine the smallest and lightest, so the van der Waals attraction — and with it the energy needed to boil the liquid — falls in the order \(\mathrm{RI > RBr > RCl > RF}\).

rows.stem:
(a) Define the following terms :
(i) Invert Sugar
(ii) Polysaccharides
(b) On the basis of structure differentiate between fibrous and globular proteins.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Invert sugar is the equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose obtained by hydrolysing sucrose. The name records a change of SIGN: sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the hydrolysis gives dextrorotatory glucose together with fructose, which is so strongly laevorotatory that it outweighs the glucose. The net rotation of the mixture is therefore to the left — inverted.

(ii) Polysaccharides are carbohydrates that give a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. They do not taste sweet and are generally insoluble in water; starch, cellulose and glycogen are the important examples.

(b) The two classes differ in how the polypeptide chains are arranged. In a FIBROUS protein the chains lie parallel to one another and are held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a thread-like structure that is insoluble in water; keratin and myosin are examples. In a GLOBULAR protein the chain coils and folds back on itself into a roughly spherical shape, and these are generally soluble in water; insulin and albumin are examples.

rows.stem:
(a) Why is glycogen known as animal starch ?
(b) Differentiate between essential amino acids and non-essential amino acids.
(c) What is the effect of denaturation on the structure of proteins ?
rows.solution:
(a) Glycogen is the form in which carbohydrate is stored in the animal body — in the liver and in muscle — and it plays the same role there that starch plays in plants. Its structure matches that use: it is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose built like amylopectin but even more highly branched, so that glucose units can be released quickly from many chain ends at once when the body needs them. Hence the name animal starch.

(b) Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise for itself and must obtain ready-made from the diet — valine, leucine and lysine among them. Non-essential amino acids are those the body can synthesise on its own, such as glycine and alanine.

(c) Denaturation destroys the SECONDARY and TERTIARY structure of a protein while leaving the PRIMARY structure intact. Heat, or a change in pH, disturbs the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the chain in its folded shape: the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds. But the peptide bonds themselves are not broken, so the sequence of amino acid residues survives. The protein nevertheless loses its biological activity, because that activity depends on the shape rather than on the sequence alone. Coagulating the white of an egg is the everyday example.
